# A closed enum's integer-form conversions are crate-private

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `3d1691a` on
`libgit2-crustify/evolution/enum-integer-form-crate-private`, awaiting its review.

## Signal

I had to work out a rule by hand that a skill should have stated, and two skills read
together leave it open.

## Evidence

`wave-186/batch-0/run-1` ported `src/cli/opt.h`'s closed enums `cli_opt_type_t` and
`cli_opt_status_t` (`Kind`, `Status` in `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`). Both are scheduled a
`port/layout` (wave 2404), which per `porting-types`' Enums section "removes that form, its
C layout: its `repr`, its discriminants and its conversions". `porting` says a later stage
changes the code that reaches the item's C form, "never the safe API its consumers use". The
precedents the tree holds are bindings, whose integer form is permanent: `tree.rs`'s
`FileMode` and `WalkMode` have public `from_raw` / `raw`, `TryFrom` / `From` and a public
`Unnamed*` error type. Copied into a port, these would be public API that the enum's
`port/layout` removes, and `ffimap api` would report it `changed`.

The batch made the conversions `pub(crate) const fn from_raw(u32) -> Option<Self>` and
`raw(self) -> u32`. No code calls them yet, because the gateways that will (`cli_opt_parse`'s
export) are later batches of the module. With warnings denied, `dead_code` then fails the
build, so each conversion carries
`#[cfg_attr(not(test), expect(dead_code, reason = "…"))]`, and an inline `equiv_priv` test
compares them with `sys::git2`'s constants.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-types`' Enums section, which the translator evolves.

## Change

crustify `3d1691a`. After "its `repr`, its discriminants and its conversions", the section
now says that the conversions are crate-private, reached only by the gateways and regions,
since the stage keeps the safe API. It also says that a conversion no crate code calls yet
carries a `dead_code` expectation that holds outside tests, and that an `equiv_priv` test
compares it with the C's constants. The change drafts its `EVOLUTION.md` entry.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands. The change was made as crustify
`3d1691a`, which also edited `EVOLUTION.md`; on 2026-11-14 it was put on the working branch's
tip as `166d8fd`, the same diff without that edit, since a change's row is drafted in its
proposal. It sits on crustify `4a0e778`, and its review reads `166d8fd`.

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a closed enum's integer-form conversions are crate-private, kept against `dead_code` until a gateway calls them | `libgit2-crustify`, `enum-integer-form-crate-private` | crustify `166d8fd` | `porting-types` has `port/layout` remove an enum's conversions while `porting` has later stages keep the safe API, and a port of enums ahead of their gateways meets `dead_code`: the batch worked out their visibility by hand | a ported closed enum whose `from_raw`/`raw` or `TryFrom`/`From` integer conversions are public, or a `port/layout` whose API stability row reports a conversion `removed` or `changed` | watched |

## Validation

No failure prompted the change, and its effect is not in doubt: this batch's `opt.rs` is
the case. It builds and lints with warnings denied, both with and without `cfg(test)`
(`clippy --all-targets`), and its `equiv_priv` tests pass under plain, ASan+UBSan and Miri.
`ffimap api` reports the enums `new`, with no public conversion for a later stage to remove.

content.content:
---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first

campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a

[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect

  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;

[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

# Evolution

providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;

  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);

# Porting types

How a scheduled C type is reimplemented in safe Rust: the type route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s; the symbols it reaches are
[`porting-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s.

---
name: porting
description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."
---

# Porting

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

## 1. FFI boundary

`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.

While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:

- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.

## 6. Enums

An enum is bound to a safe Rust type over the constants bindgen generates for it:

- a closed enum is a Rust enum, with a variant for each of its constants;
- an enum whose constants C combines as flags is a `#[repr(transparent)]` newtype over its
  integer type, with an associated constant for each of its constants and the bitwise
  operators, since a combination is no variant; and
- an enum without a name has no type to bind: its constants become constants of its
  integer type.

Beneath a closed enum's safe type sits its integer form, the interop layer C needs: a
`#[repr]` over the enum's integer type, as bindgen gives it, each constant's value its
variant's discriminant, and the conversions through which its values cross the boundary
as that integer. A value from C is converted fallibly where it enters Rust, since C may
pass one the enum does not name, which a Rust enum may not hold: such a value takes the
path the C gives an invalid value, or an error of the safe API where it gives none. A
binding keeps the integer form for good, since C implements what produces and consumes
the enum's values.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

## 4. Formatting

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
----
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
----
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.
-----
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

content.content:
A batch validates its own change on its own base first. Its rebase onto the integration
branch, under the landing lock that [`versioning`](../../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section
describes, then combines that change with the work landed since: the gates run again are
those that could catch a regression the combination introduces, judged from what the
batch's change and the rebased-in changes touch and how they could interact. A gate that
neither side's changes could affect keeps the result it had, and a rebase that conflicts
makes the resolved tree new work of the batch's own.

A `port` batch changes no C: its gates are those above, run against the variants with its
module's export feature off, so that the ported Rust is tested beside the C it replaces.
It also checks and lints the safe crate with that feature on, which compiles the module's
gateway without linking it, and each export is checked at compile time against the raw
binding of the C declaration it replaces, so that a signature that drifts from C's fails
to build.

A module's switch removes its translation unit, and the C tests tied to it that reach
its internals, from `c/`, rebuilds the variants from the C that remains and deletes the
module's export feature, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes. Its gates are a module's end's, in campaign mode over the rebuilt variants, and
the target's remaining C tests, which link the remaining C and the safe crate's Rust static
library, so that the C reaches the ported module through its exports: the module's tied C
tests that use only its public API among them, as the porting workflow's Tests follow
their modules section describes. Before a tied C test leaves, the cases none of the
module's `unit_pub` tests carries over are listed, as [`testing`](../SKILL.md)'s C tests
carried over section describes.

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:
  - the items a later batch or review reshaped; and

- **Not taken yet.**
  - both paired measures;
  - the departures that state their reason, against the departures a review had to find; and
  - whether an item translated twice took the same shape both times.

content.content:
# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 1. Safety

No undefined behaviour is reachable from safe Rust. The unsafe code that remains sits in its
regions, and is sound for every input.

### The unsafe surface

- **Measure.** What a deterministic scan counts on each landing:
  - raw pointers and `unsafe fn`s on the public API;
  - unsafe lines and raw dereferences; and
  - unsafe code outside its regions.

  The first two fall as a module goes from wrapped to ported and through its later stages.
  The third is zero throughout.
- **Paired with** soundness, below. Calling an unsound function safe takes an obligation off
  the API, and so lowers this measure.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 2. Equivalence

The Rust keeps the C's specified behaviour, not its bugs. The specified behaviour is what
the C's documentation, tests and consumers rely on.

- **Measure.**
  - The target's own tests passing over the Rust at each switch, against their recorded
    baseline.
  - The inputs and states on which the Rust is compared with the C it replaces, with no
    difference left unexplained.
  - The differences made on purpose, each documented and held by a test.

---
name: evolution-record
description: "The record of the changes that landed in Crustify and its tools, `EVOLUTION.md`: its rows, their recurrence signals and statuses, when the watched rows are read, and how evolution itself evolves from the record. Read before drafting a change's row, writing or reading the record, or proposing a change to the evolution protocol."
---

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

---
name: authoring
description: "How Crustify itself is organized: skills, roles, tool skills and the plugin, where each kind of text goes, and the language every text is written in. Read before changing Crustify, filing a proposal or a lesson, or writing a task message for an agent."
---

# Authoring

How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
and no two copies drift apart.

## 1. Layers

Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:

| layer | where | voice | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |

Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
hold illustrations, not rules.

The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.

### 1.1 Skills

A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.

Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.

A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.

A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
- `compose.py`, which generates the agents (`compose.py build`).

The generated files are committed, and regenerated whenever `agents/` or
`system-prompt.md` changes.

## 5. Language

Programmers and agents read Crustify's texts and a campaign's, so they are written plainly,
as the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style)
describes: one term per thing, short sentences, a condition before its consequence, lists for
parallel items. A rule keeps its reason, since agents generalize from reasons. A rewrite keeps
every fact of the old text, which its review checks. The voice rules of [Layers](#1-layers)
stay: a skill describes, an agent instructs.

  their modules' batches revisit them; they are not wrong, since the standard family is the
  C library's heap, but they repeat a binding by hand.

## reftable's error type is `basics::Error`, which `error.c`'s port takes over

- **Rule.** Rust reports reftable's error codes as `deps::reftable::basics::Error`, and no
  other reftable module defines an error type of its own. The batch that ports
  `enum reftable_error` (`deps/reftable/error.c`, wave 217 under planner run 12's numbering)
  makes that type the enum's port, not a second one: it moves `Error` to
  `src/libgit2/deps/reftable/error.rs` with a variant per constant of
  `deps/reftable/reftable-error.h`, each anchored to its constant, keeps `Other(c_int)` for
  codes outside the enum and `from_code` / `code`, gives `Display` `reftable_error_str`'s text,
  and leaves `pub use super::error::Error;` in `basics.rs`, so that `basics.rs`'s callers and
  tests do not change.
- **Evidence.** `deps/reftable/basics.c` returns `REFTABLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY_ERROR` and
  `REFTABLE_FORMAT_ERROR`, yet was scheduled (wave 169, foundational, now integrated) with no

  `crustify/evolution/reftable-error-wrapped-ahead-of-basics`).

content.content:
## 8. Incremental migration without breaking consumers

A codebase moves to Rust one module at a time. Every landing builds and passes its gates. No
consumer breaks: a C or Rust consumer's code does not change as what it consumes is wrapped,
ported or moves through its later stages.

- **Measure.**
  - The items whose API changed or went after their first landing, each with its reason.
  - The landed trees that failed a gate.
  - The target's test baseline, which moves only by the cases carried over.
- **Paired with** Idiomatic Rust's measure of C forms on the public API. An API that never
  changes because it stayed C's breaks no one and serves no one.

### The order

- **Measure.** The batches that met a dependency not yet landed, and waited for it, rewrote
  around it or reached past its wrapper.

  Items land after what they depend on. Where the order cuts a cycle, an item lands after
  the binding of what it depends on. That order is how this goal is met, and Safety's and
  Performance's with it: a consumer written once, over a boundary written once.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:
  - the items a later batch or review reshaped; and
  - the conventions findings a later tier makes on an item an earlier review passed.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - both paired measures;
  - the departures that state their reason, against the departures a review had to find; and
  - whether an item translated twice took the same shape both times.

**Verdict: rejected.** Three fixes are required. Two of them can be made by removing or scoping text rather than adding rules. The change does not weaken a check, and it touches no protected path. I changed and landed nothing, so the verdict still needs recording in the proposal's Review section.

The core rule is sound and well placed, but it conflicts with `porting` for enums that were wrapped before their port. This campaign meets that case at wave 1024.

## Required fixes

1. **It contradicts `porting`'s FFI boundary section and Goal 8 for an enum wrapped before its port.**
   - `porting` says that when a wrapper already exists, "the port keeps that wrapper's safe API". The new sentence makes the conversions crate-private in every case.
   - In this campaign, `tree.rs`'s `FileMode`, `WalkMode` and `UpdateAction` are wrapped with public `from_raw`/`raw`, `TryFrom`/`From` and `Unnamed*` errors.
   - The public-interface suite uses them: `tests/ub_safe/src/libgit2/tree.rs:19,36` and `tests/ub_safe/src/libgit2/signature/types.rs:489`.
   - All three are ported at wave 1024, with `port/layout` at waves 1633 (`WalkMode`) and 2381 (`FileMode`). The translator at wave 1024 gets two rules that disagree.
   - The proposal calls these precedents "bindings, whose integer form is permanent". `schedule.json` contradicts that, and the error is how the conflict was missed.
   - **Fix (scoping, a few words):** limit the rule to the conversions a port writes for an enum no wrapper already gave a safe API. Correct the evidence sentence too.

2. **The `dead_code` expectation is stated wrongly for the caller the sentence itself expects, the gateway.**
   - The gateway compiles only under its module's export feature, and `testing-gates` has a port batch lint with that feature both off and on.
   - I reproduced this in a scratch crate:
     - Before any caller exists, `cfg_attr(not(test), expect(dead_code))` passes both lints.
     - Once a feature-gated gateway calls the conversion, keeping the expectation fails the feature-on lint ("lint expectation is unfulfilled").
     - Removing it instead fails the feature-off lint ("never used").
     - Only `not(any(test, feature = …))` passes both.
   - This module already met it: batch 5 (`c62dee857`) worked out that form by hand for the `cli_opt_foreach` export.
   - **Fix (removal):** delete the sentence "A conversion that no code of the crate calls yet … compares it with the C's constants." `toolchain`'s Lints section already says an exception is a local `#[expect]` that fails once it is no longer needed. The alternative is to add the feature condition, which is more text.

3. **The drafted row's recurrence signal would fire on cases the change doesn't cover.**
   - Wave 1024 keeping tree's public conversions, as `porting` requires, would match it.
   - So would the `port/layout`s at 1633 and 2381 removing them.
   - Either would mark the row `recurred` falsely.
   - **Fix:** scope the signal to enums whose first safe API came from a port. If fix 2 removes the sentence, drop "kept against `dead_code` until a gateway calls them" from the row's change text.

## Not required (listed apart)

- **Terms:** "a gateway or a region" names one thing twice, since the gateway *is* the `ffi_export` region. `porting`'s own wording is "in its module's unsafe regions". `pub(crate)` is still the right visibility, because other modules' regions convert too (for example, `index.rs:3172` converts `FileMode`).
- **Formatting:** the edited paragraph wasn't re-wrapped, so one line runs about 150 columns.
- **Missing goal:** the proposal doesn't name its goal and measure, which the `evolution` skill's Proposals section requires. It serves Goal 8 ("items whose API changed or went after their first landing") and Consistency.
- **Stale status:** the proposal's status line still names `3d1691a`.
- **Root gap, worth its own proposal:** a wrap of a closed enum whose port is planned should also keep its conversions crate-private. `binding-types` now says "a binding keeps the integer form for good", so tree's `port/layout`s will meet this conflict whatever this change says.
- **Placement:** the `dead_code`-ahead-of-callers pattern is general. Batch 4 used it for four parser helpers, so if it is stated anywhere it belongs in `toolchain` or `porting`, not under Enums.
- **Test kind:** an `equiv_priv` test of constants stretches `testing`'s "internal routine" wording, but contradicts nothing.

## Checks and evidence

- **No target names:** the diff states no rule in the target's names.
- **Same diff:** `166d8fd`'s skill diff is identical to `3d1691a`'s, minus the `EVOLUTION.md` edit.
- **Duplicates:** the campaign's index and the record hold no duplicate of this proposal and no recurrence of a landed row.
- **The batch's records** (`wave-186/batch-0/run-1/stream.jsonl`, `api-diff.json`):
  - `clippy --all-targets -D warnings` passed.
  - The `cli::opt` tests passed, plain and under Miri.
  - `ffimap api` reports every item `new`, with no public conversion.
  - An ASan run was made, but I did not confirm its result.
- **Correction to the evidence:** the first callers of the conversions were `ffi_import` accessors from batch 2's wrap (`fe6b85bfa`), not the gateway. The signal still holds.
- **Rerun:** not cheap enough to do here, so it wasn't done. The `git2` link unit builds only in campaign mode, against a CMake/Ninja variant built from that commit's C. The current variants are post-switch, and the build at `8a149ac08` against them fails with "cannot link crustify/liblibgit2_crustify.a". The scratch crate stood in for the lint behaviour the rule rests on.
- **Cleanup:** the scratch worktree, target dir and repro crate under `crustify/tmp/` are removed, and `crustify/builds` is intact.

I proposed and recorded nothing myself.
